16th Century.historical_context: Formation of Imperial Mughal atelier under Akbar, synthesis of Persian Safavid masters (Mir Sayyid Ali, Abd al-Samad) with indigenous Indian artists.
stylistic_markers: Vibrant narrative dynamism, diagonal crowded compositions full of movement and action
Multiple artists collaborating on single folios (outline by master, coloring by assistant)
Persian high horizon lines and tiered spatial planes blending with Indian earthy vigor
Vigorous, bold brushwork capturing architectural construction, battle scenes, and hunts
Illustrations of epic historical chronicles (Hamzanama, Tutinama, Akbarnama, Razmnama)
16th Century.pigments_materials: Coarser mineral pigments, organic dyes, hand-made Sialkot paper, vigorous burnishing.

Early 17th Century.historical_context: Shift from collective manuscript production to individualized connoisseurship and single-page album (muraqqa) paintings.
stylistic_markers: Supreme psychological realism, acute naturalistic observation, and refined delicate brushwork
Extraordinary flora and fauna studies (birds, animals, flowers) commissioned by Jahangir
European Renaissance influence: subtle chiaroscuro, golden divine halos, winged cherubs in skies
Individual master artist attribution prominently recorded by the Emperor himself
Muraqqa albums with sumptuous wide calligraphic and illuminated floral borders
Early 17th Century.pigments_materials: Ultra-refined lapis lazuli, malachite, cinnabar, shell gold ink (hallkari).

Mid 17th Century.historical_context: Imperial grandeur, architectural perfection, courtly ritual and frozen formal majesty.
stylistic_markers: Strict formal symmetry, imperial stillness, and crystalline architectural clarity
En-face and strict profile court portraits with jewel-encrusted thrones and weapons
Opulent application of heavy gold leaf (gilding) and polished surface finish
Diminished dynamic narrative action in favor of ceremonial darbar scenes and romantic night terraces
Padshahnama manuscript illustrating royal court rituals and historical events
Mid 17th Century.pigments_materials: Heavy gold leaf, powdered pearls, intense burnishing producing porcelain-like sheen.

Late 17th Century.historical_context: Decline of imperial Mughal patronage; migration of court artists to regional Rajput, Pahari, and Deccani centers.
stylistic_markers: More austere, subdued color palettes at the Mughal court; strict formal portraiture
Flowering of regional styles in Rajasthan and Deccan enriched by displaced imperial masters
Simpler backgrounds with pale celadon green or grey washes replacing opulent architectural gold
Increased production of religious, mythological, and Ragamala series in regional ateliers
Late 17th Century.pigments_materials: Mix of indigenous regional pigments with refined Mughal techniques.

18th Century.period_name: 18th Century (c. 1707 - 1799, Later Mughal, Rajput, and Pahari Flowering)
18th Century.historical_context: Golden age of Rajput (Mewar, Bundi, Kota, Kishangarh) and early Pahari (Basohli, Guler, Kangra) schools.
stylistic_markers: Rich emotional expression, lyrical lines, and profound romantic and devotional themes
Spectacular Ragamala, Barahmasa (seasons), and Gitagovinda series
Kishangarh's romantic vision under Savant Singh; Kangra's supreme poetic beauty under Sansar Chand
Intense color grounds in Rajasthan contrasted with serene pastel hillscapes in Himachal
18th Century.pigments_materials: Locally sourced mineral clays, peori yellow, kajal black, gold powders on layered wasli paper.
